newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan war heats up after ceasefire talks fail.
newsitem.headline: Afghan war heats up after ceasefire talks fail.

text.p: Anti-Taleban forces struck at the purist Islamic militia from the air and on the ground on Sunday, expanding Afghanistan's latest war as Kabul's new rulers confirmed ceasefire talks had failed.
Fighting on the front north of Kabul was heavy all day and was still raging as darkness approached, witnesses said.

They said the two sides exchanged heavy salvoes of rockets, artillery and mortar fire and both sent in bombers. The Taleban also used a helicopter gunship in the fighting over a line of hills across a plain 25 to 30 km (15 to 20 miles) north of Kabul.
Taleban fighters near the front line said they had fought back the combined forces of northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum and former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.

Taleban kept control of the strategic De Sabz pass, 30 km (20 miles) north of Kabul on Sunday despite a strong assault by ousted Afghan government forces. Fighting died down in the afternoon but intermittent shells and rockets could still be seen landing on the pass.
Asked if former government forces under ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood had taken the pass, Masood's spokesman, Doctor Abdullah, said: "No, not yet."

If the northern allies could break through the hills -- and repeated attempts by Masood's men failed last week -- they would have a relatively clear run over gently undulating land to the edge of the Kabul valley.

They launched their new bid to punch through the Taleban lines shortly after warplanes swept over Kabul twice on a Saturday night lit by a full moon, aimed bombs at the airport and set off a furious stream of anti-aircaft fire.

The first screamed in low over the capital just before a 9 p.m. (1630 GMT) curfew. The second hit three hours later and its bomb struck a city centre park, shredding trees and shattering the windows of about 40 nearby shops, but hurting no one.
Following the first night air raids in 17 years of war in Afghanistan, another tried again to hit the airport on the northeastern edge of the capital on Sunday morning.
Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told a news conference the raids, which he said were ordered by Dostum, caused no damage or casualties.

He also blamed Dostum for the failure of ceasefire talks brokered by Pakistan and United Nations envoy Norbert Holl by demanding the demilitarisation of Kabul, a condition Murtaqi called irrational. "The negotiations were a failure. They chose the path of fighting," he added.

Mutaqi said the Taleban were ready for talks that would spread Islam's stern Sharia law across the whole country. "They should accept the establishment of an Islamic system and obey Islamic principles," he said of the other factions.
Dostujm and Masood allied formally two weeks ago after two years of bitter estrangement and Dostum sent tanks, artillery and men to Masood's front line on the plain north of Kabul.
The largely ethnic Pashtun Taleban started using combat aircraft last week to help hold their lines and in one raid a Taleban bomb killed at least 14 civilians in the front line village of Kalakan.
On Thursday, the Taleban signalled an end to any lingering hopes of a ceasefire by attacking Dostum directly in the remote northwestern province of Badghis.

The Taleban said they had taken the province and pushed into neighbouring Faryab province. On Sunday they said their forces were pushing towards the provincial capital of Maimana, where Dostum has a major base.
If they took that city, then they could threaten Dostum's capital of Mazar-i-Sharif.

There have been no reliable independent reports of the fighting in the northwest, but a Masood spokesman implicitly denied the loss of Badghis on Saturday, saying fighting was going on, mostly involving infantry and armoured vehicles.
